title: Most Romans deny natural or congruous merit of first grace
source_text: LVI. Verum ipsi Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, aut eorum saltem plurimi, nullas ejusmodi dispositiones agnoscere videntur. Quandoquidem profitentur cum Concilio Tridentino, nihil eorum quae praecedunt justificationem, justificationis gratiam pro-mereri; & illas qualescunque dispositiones tribuunt, non naturalibus liberi arbitrii viri-bus, sed auxilio gratiae excitantis & praevenientis. Testis sit unus pro omnibus Tho-mas Stapletonus Anglus, Protestantium hostis infestissimus, & acerrimus justitiae in-haerentis defensor, quique omnium accuratissime doctrinam Pontificiorum de justifi-catione tractavisse videtur. Is enim Prolegomenis in librum quintum de Justificatione, postquam enumeravit varias dispositiones ordinarie ad illam requisitas, juxta Con-cilii Tridentini mentem, inter alia duo monet. Unum est, Non per opera tanquam a nostris viribus profecta, sed tanquam effectus gratiae praevenientis, & adjuvantis, nos disponi ad primam justitiam. Alterum, Non sic disponi nos per ista opera, ut mereamur primam justitiam, ne quidem ex congruo. Et postea adhuc diligenter in-culcat, opera pure moralia, & solius naturae viribus producta, ad justitiam Christia-nam non disponere, neque praeparare; nec ullo modo quicquam, quod ad vitam, aut gloriam Spiritualem pertinet mereri. Ac denique notat ex dispositionibus non con-sequi ipsam justitiam, tanquam ex sua causa effectum. Qua in re plurimos Docto-res Ecclesiae Romanae ipsi adstipulantes hic citare liceret, sed brevitatis causa superse-demus.
pass_a_gloss: But the doctors of the Roman Church themselves, or at least most of them, seem to acknowledge no such dispositions. Since they profess with the Council of Trent that nothing of those things which precede justification merits the grace of justification; and they ascribe those dispositions of whatever kind not to the natural powers of free will, but to the help of exciting and preventing grace. Let one witness for all be Thomas Stapleton the Englishman, a most hostile enemy of the Protestants and a most keen defender of inherent righteousness, and who seems to have treated the Papists' doctrine of justification most accurately of all. For he, in the Prolegomena to the fifth book on Justification, after enumerating various dispositions ordinarily required for it according to the mind of the Council of Trent, among other things warns of two. One is: that we are disposed to the first righteousness not by works as proceeding from our powers, but as effects of preventing and assisting grace. The other: that we are not so disposed by those works that we merit the first righteousness, not even by congruity. And afterward he still carefully inculcates that purely moral works, produced by the powers of nature alone, do not dispose or prepare for Christian righteousness; nor in any way merit anything that pertains to spiritual life or glory. And finally he notes that from dispositions the righteousness itself does not follow as an effect from its cause. In which matter we might here cite many doctors of the Roman Church agreeing with him, but for brevity's sake we forbear.
pass_b_english: Most Roman doctors deny such meritorious/natural dispositions—Trent: nothing preceding merits justification grace; dispositions are from preventing grace.
Stapleton: not from our powers; not even de congruo; pure moral works do not prepare for Christian justice.
